readingInstruction: Read Psalm 46. It is the psalm behind Martin Luther’s hymn “A Mighty Fortress.” Notice the three stanzas separated by “Selah,” each ending in the refrain, “The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress.”
settingTheScene: Psalm 46 is a song of the sons of Korah, probably written after a great deliverance, perhaps the rescue of Jerusalem from Sennacherib’s army in 701 BC (Isaiah 36-37). It sets the stability of God’s city against the chaos of earthquakes and storms and the raging of nations. In our reading of Revelation, it provides a counterpoint to the plagues and wars: in the middle of upheaval, the people of God have a river, a city, and a God who is present.
observation: “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (v. 1).
“Therefore we will not fear though the earth gives way” (v. 2).
“There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God” (v. 4).
“God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns” (v. 5).
“The nations rage, the kingdoms totter; he utters his voice, the earth melts” (v. 6).
“The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress” (v. 7).
“He makes wars cease to the end of the earth” (v. 9).
“Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth!” (v. 10).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with a statement of faith: “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.” He is not a distant helper; he is very present, close at hand. The consequence is: “Therefore we will not fear though the earth gives way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea, though its waters roar and foam, though the mountains tremble at its swelling.” This is the worst-case scenario: creation itself coming apart. Even then, God’s people do not fear. It is like many of the images in Revelation, where mountains move and seas turn to blood.

The second stanza turns to the city of God. “There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High.” Jerusalem had no river, only a gentle spring, Gihon. The river is symbolic, a picture of God’s presence bringing life and gladness. In Ezekiel 47 and in Revelation 22:1-2, this river becomes a great reality flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. “God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns.” While the sea roars and mountains shake, the city is safe, because God dwells in it. “The nations rage, the kingdoms totter; he utters his voice, the earth melts.” Notice the same verb used for the nations raging in Psalm 2. Their raging is answered by a word from God.

The third stanza invites us to look at God’s works: “Come, behold the works of the LORD, how he has brought desolations on the earth. He makes wars cease to the end of the earth; he breaks the bow and shatters the spear; he burns the chariots with fire.” The Lord ends wars, which we long to see. And then the famous command: “Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth!” “Be still” means to cease striving, to let go. It is addressed to God’s people in trouble, and also to the raging nations. The way to face the chaos is not to panic but to be still, and know that he is God.

The refrain is the center: “The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress.” The Lord of hosts commands every army, and the God of Jacob is the God who stayed faithful to a flawed man. He is both powerful and personal. And in Christ, he is Immanuel, God with us. At the end of Revelation, the same truth is proclaimed: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (21:3). The city of God, with its river, is the final home of his people.
connection: Isaiah 8:8-10 and 37:33-38 relate to Immanuel and the deliverance of Jerusalem. Genesis 2:10-14 and Ezekiel 47:1-12 describe rivers of life. Revelation 21:2-3 and 22:1-2 show the city and river. Psalm 48 and 87 also celebrate the city of God. Psalm 2 uses the same word for nations raging. Matthew 1:23 gives the name Immanuel. Exodus 14:13-14 shows God fighting for a people who are still. Isaiah 30:15 and 40:31 speak of quietness and strength. Hebrews 12:22-28 speaks of an unshakable kingdom. Romans 8:31-39 expresses similar confidence.
application:
Take five minutes of silence today, and put a name on the thing you are anxious about. Then say, “Be still, and know that I am God.”

Memorize verse 1. It can be prayed in any trouble.

Name a place in your life where the ground is shaking (health, work, relationships). Place it in the hands of the God who is a very present help.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you fear, and say that he is your refuge and strength.
Be still, and know that he is God.
Thank him that he is with you.
